# Microbiome data science {#sec-microbiome-in-bioconductor}

This work - [**Orchestrating Microbiome Analysis with
Bioconductor**](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OMA/) [@OMA] - contributes
novel methods and educational resources for microbiome data science. It
aims to teach the grammar of Bioconductor workflows in the context of
microbiome data science. We show, through concrete examples, how to use
the latest developments and data analytical strategies in R/Bioconductor
for the manipulation, analysis, and reproducible reporting of
hierarchical, heterogeneous, and multi-modal microbiome profiling data.
The data science methodology is tightly integrated with the broader
R/Bioconductor ecosystem. The support for modularity and
interoperability is key to efficient resource sharing and collaborative
development both within and across research fields.

## Bioconductor {#sec-bioconductor}

[Bioconductor](https://bioconductor.org/) is a project that focuses on the development of
high-quality open research software for life sciences [@Gentleman2004;
@Huber2015]. The software packages are primarily coded in R, and they
undergo continuous testing and peer review to ensure high quality.

![](figures/bioconductor_logo_cmyk.svg){width="40%" fig-alt="Bioconductor logo."}

Central to the software in Bioconductor are data containers, which
provide a structured presentation of data. A data container consists of
slots that are dedicated to certain type of data, for example, to
abundance table and sample metadata. Biological data is often complex
and multidimensional, making data containers particularly beneficial.
There are several key advantages to using data containers:

- **Ease of handling:** Data subsetting and bookkeeping become more
straightforward.
- **Development efficiency:** Developers can create efficient methods,
knowing the data will be in a consistent format.
- **User accessibility:** Users can easily apply complex methods to
their data.

The most common data container in Bioconductor is
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("SummarizedExperiment")`. It is further expanded
to fulfill needs of certain application field.
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("SummarizedExperiment")` and its derivatives,
have already been widely adopted in microbiome research, single cell
sequencing, and in other fields, allowing rapid adoption and the
extension of emerging data science techniques across application
domains. See [@sec-data-containers] for more details on how to handle
data containers from the `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("SummarizedExperiment")` family.

The Bioconductor microbiome data science framework consists of:

- **Data containers**, designed to organize multi-assay microbiome data
- **R/Bioconductor packages** that provide dedicated methods
- **Community** of users and developers

These components build on each other (@fig-ecosystem).

![Data containers are central in
Bioconductor.](figures/ecosystem.png){#fig-ecosystem width="50%"
fig-alt="Three nested ellipses: data at the core, surrounded by packages,
surrounded by community."}

If you are new to R or Bioconductor, the following
[Carpentries](https://carpentries.org/) lessons, contributed by Bioconductor,
provide the basic background:

- [Introduction to data analysis with R and Bioconductor](https://carpentries-incubator.github.io/bioc-intro/)
- [Introduction to the Bioconductor project](https://carpentries-incubator.github.io/bioc-project/)

## Microbiome data science {#sec-microbiome-bioc}

While microbiota is used to refer micro-organisms within well-specified
area, microbiome means microbiota and their genetic material
[@Marchesi2015]. Because the complex nature of the microbiome data,
computational methods are essential in microbiome research.

The `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("phyloseq")` data container has been dominant
in the microbiome field within Bioconductor over the past decade
[@McMurdie2013]. However, the data container no longer adequately meets
the needs of current research, as it was originally developed for 16S
sequencing data. For instance, incorporating diverse multi-omics datasets
has become increasingly common.

An optimal data container (@fig-optimal-container) should efficiently
store and manage large volumes of data, including modified or transformed
copies of different measurements. Furthermore, it should seamlessly integrate into the
broader ecosystem of Bioconductor, minimizing duplication of effort and
facilitating interoperability with other tools and packages.

![Requirements for an optimal data container for microbiome
data.](figures/optimal_data_container.png){#fig-optimal-container width="50%"
fig-alt="Requirements: multiple assays with seamless interlinking,
hierarchical data, side information, optimized for speed and memory, and
integrated with other applications and frameworks."}

`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("TreeSummarizedExperiment")` was developed to address
these requirements [@Huang2021]. The [OMA microbiome data science framework](https://microbiome.github.io/)
was subsequently built around the
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("TreeSummarizedExperiment")` data container [@sec-ecosystem].

## Open data science {#sec-open-data}

Open data science emphasizes sharing code and, where feasible, data
alongside results [@Shetty2019]. Utilizing Bioconductor tools
facilitates the development of efficient and reproducible data science
workflows. Enhanced transparency in research accelerates scientific
progress. As open science is a fundamental concept in microbiome
research, this book aims to educate readers about reproducible reporting
practices.

### Reproducible reporting with Quarto {#sec-reproducible-reporting}

A reproducible report combines the text, the code and the results of an
analysis in a single document. When the data or the code change, the report
is rendered again, and all numbers, figures and tables are updated
automatically. This avoids errors from copying results by hand, and it shows
others exactly how the results were obtained.

[Quarto](https://quarto.org/) is an open-source system for writing such
reports. A Quarto document is a text file with the extension `.qmd`, and it
can be rendered, for example, into an HTML page, a PDF or a Word document.
This book is also written with Quarto: each chapter is a Quarto document, and
the code in the chapters is run every time the book is built. Quarto is
included in RStudio, where you can create a new document from
**File > New File > Quarto Document** and render it with the **Render**
button.

A Quarto document has three main parts:

- **YAML header**, between the two `---` lines at the top of the document. It
sets, for example, the title and the output format.
- **Text**, written in [Markdown](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html).
For instance, `#` starts a heading, `-` starts a list item and
`[text](url)` creates a link.
- **Code chunks**, which start with ```` ```{r} ```` and end with
```` ``` ````. The code is run when the document is rendered, and its output
is shown below the chunk. Chunk options at the beginning of the chunk start
with `#|`. They give the chunk a label and control, for instance, whether the
code is shown (`echo`) and what the caption of a figure is (`fig-cap`). R
code can also be placed inside the text, so that a number in a sentence is
calculated from the data.

Below is a small Quarto document that loads example data with
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("mia")`. You can copy it into a new Quarto document in
RStudio and render it. If the rendering succeeds, Quarto and the
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("mia")` package are working.

````markdown
---
title: "My first analysis"
format: html
---

## Data

We use the `GlobalPatterns` dataset from the mia package.

```{{r}}
#| label: load-data
library(mia)
data("GlobalPatterns", package = "mia")
tse <- GlobalPatterns
tse
```

The data has `r knitr::inline_expr("nrow(tse)")` features and
`r knitr::inline_expr("ncol(tse)")` samples.
````

Most of the code in this book can be copied into a Quarto document in the
same way, which makes Quarto a convenient way to follow the book and to keep
your own analyses reproducible. More material on Quarto is listed in
[@sec-quarto].

::: callout-tip
## Summary

- Bioconductor is a large ecosystem for bioinformatics.
- Data containers are fundamental in Bioconductor.
- `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("SummarizedExperiment")` is the most common data
container in Bioconductor.
- Quarto documents combine text, code and results into reproducible reports.
:::

## Exercises {#sec-microbiome-in-bioconductor-exercises}

Exercises 3-6 build a small reproducible report on the alpha diversity of
the `GlobalPatterns` dataset, so solve them in order. Before starting them,
read [@sec-reproducible-reporting]. You do not need to write the analysis
code yourself: you copy it from this book, and focus on how the Quarto
document is built and how its output is controlled. Try to solve each
exercise yourself before opening the solution.

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 1: Data containers

**Goal:** Understand what data containers are and why they are central in
Bioconductor.

Answer the following questions without writing any code.
[@sec-bioconductor] and [@sec-microbiome-bioc] will help you.

1. What is a data container? Name two types of data that are stored in its
slots.

2. List the three advantages of data containers that are described in this
chapter.

3. Imagine that you store the abundance table and the sample metadata as two
separate tables. You remove three samples from the abundance table but forget
to remove them from the sample metadata. What problem does this cause? How
does a data container help to avoid it?

4. Which data container is the most common in Bioconductor? Which data
container is the OMA framework built around?

5. Why does the `phyloseq` data container no longer meet the needs of
current microbiome research?

6. What are the three parts of the Bioconductor microbiome data science
framework?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

1. A data container is an object that stores data in a structured way. It
consists of slots, each dedicated to a certain type of data, for example the
abundance table and the sample metadata.

2. The advantages are ease of handling (subsetting and bookkeeping are more
straightforward), development efficiency (developers can rely on a consistent
data format), and user accessibility (users can easily apply complex methods
to their data).

3. The two tables no longer describe the same samples, and the sample
metadata can be matched to the wrong samples in later analyses. A data
container keeps the abundance table and the sample metadata linked. When you
subset the container, all its parts are subsetted at the same time, so they
stay matched.

4. `SummarizedExperiment` is the most common data container in Bioconductor.
The OMA framework is built around `TreeSummarizedExperiment`.

5. `phyloseq` was originally developed for 16S sequencing data. It does not
adequately support, for example, multi-omics datasets, which have become
increasingly common.

6. Data containers, R/Bioconductor packages that provide dedicated methods,
and a community of users and developers.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 2: Bioconductor website

**Goal:** Learn to navigate the Bioconductor website and to find information
about packages.

1. Go to the [Bioconductor website](https://bioconductor.org/).

2. Open the "Packages" section and go to the list of software packages.

3. Use the biocViews categories to list the packages in the category
"Microbiome". Note how many packages are listed. The number grows over time,
so any current number is a correct answer.

4. Open the page of the `mia` package. Which version of `mia` does the page
describe? Is it the release or the devel version? How can you tell?

5. On the same page, find the installation instructions, the vignettes and
the reference manual of `mia`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

3. The packages of the "Microbiome" category are listed on the biocViews
page. Any current number of packages is a correct answer.

4. The version is shown in the "Version" field of the package page. The page
tells whether it describes the release or the devel version. The address of
the page also contains either `release` or `devel`.

5. The installation instructions are under "Installation". The vignettes and
the reference manual are listed under "Documentation".

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 3: Create a Quarto document

**Goal:** Learn to create and render a Quarto document, and to write text
with Markdown.

1. Open RStudio and create a new Quarto document from
**File > New File > Quarto Document**. Remove the example content that
RStudio adds to the new document.

2. Copy the example document from [@sec-reproducible-reporting] into your
document. Save the file, for example as `report.qmd`, and render it with the
**Render** button. If RStudio asks to install packages, accept. If the
rendering fails, check that the `mia` package is installed.

3. Change the title in the YAML header to `"Alpha diversity in
GlobalPatterns"` and render the document again.

4. At the end of the document, add a section with the heading
`## Alpha diversity`. Under it, write a sentence that explains that alpha
diversity measures the diversity within each sample.

5. Under the sentence, add a link to the Alpha diversity chapter
([@sec-alpha-diversity]) with the syntax `[text](url)`. You can copy the
address of the chapter from your browser. Render the document.

**Useful resources:** [@sec-reproducible-reporting],
[Markdown basics](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

Your document should look similar to the following:

````markdown
---
title: "Alpha diversity in GlobalPatterns"
format: html
---

## Data

We use the `GlobalPatterns` dataset from the mia package.

```{{r}}
#| label: load-data
library(mia)
data("GlobalPatterns", package = "mia")
tse <- GlobalPatterns
tse
```

The data has `r knitr::inline_expr("nrow(tse)")` features and
`r knitr::inline_expr("ncol(tse)")` samples.

## Alpha diversity

Alpha diversity measures the diversity within each sample. The methods are
explained in the
[Alpha diversity chapter](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OMA/pages/alpha_diversity.html)
of the OMA book.
````

In the rendered document, the headings are shown as section titles, the
inline code is replaced by the numbers of features and samples, and the link
is clickable.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 4: Add code from the book

**Goal:** Learn to add code chunks and inline code to a Quarto document, and
to see how the results update automatically.

Continue with the document from Exercise 3.

1. Go to [@sec-estimate-diversity]. Copy the whole code chunk that
calculates the alpha diversity indices with `addAlpha()`. Paste it into a new
code chunk at the end of your document. You can insert a chunk with
**Ctrl + Alt + I** (Windows, Linux) or **Cmd + Option + I** (Mac). The chunk
loads the data again, which does no harm.

2. Go to [@sec-plot-diversity]. Copy the whole code chunk that plots the
observed richness by sample type (@fig-alpha-richness) into a second code
chunk, and render the document.

3. Under the figure, write the sentence "The median observed richness is X.",
where X is calculated with inline R code from `tse$observed_richness`. Render
the document.

4. In the `addAlpha()` call, change the detection threshold from
`detection = 10` to `detection = 0` and render the document again. Which parts
of the report change? Did you need to edit them by hand?

**Useful resources:** [@sec-reproducible-reporting],
[@sec-estimate-diversity], [@sec-plot-diversity]

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

The new part of the document should look similar to the following:

````markdown
```{{r}}
# First, let's load some example data.
library(mia)
data("GlobalPatterns")
tse <- GlobalPatterns

# The 'index' parameter allows computing multiple diversity indices
# simultaneously. Without specification, four standard indices are calculated:
# dbp_dominance, faith_diversity, observed_richness, and shannon_diversity.
tse <- addAlpha(
    tse,
    assay.type = "counts",
    detection = 10
)

# Check some of the first values in colData
tse$observed_richness |> head()
tse$shannon_diversity |> head()
```

```{{r}}
library(miaViz)
plotBoxplot(
    tse,
    col.var = "observed_richness",
    x = "SampleType",
    colour.by = "Final_Barcode"
) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
    labs(x = "Sample types", y = expression(Richness[observed_richness]))
```

The median observed richness is
`r knitr::inline_expr("median(tse$observed_richness)")`.
````

4. The detection threshold affects which features are counted as observed, so
the richness values change. Both the figure and the sentence are updated
automatically when the document is rendered, without any manual editing. This
is the main benefit of reproducible reporting.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 5: Control the output

**Goal:** Learn to control with chunk options how the code and its output are
shown in the rendered document.

Continue with the document from Exercise 4. Change the detection threshold
back to `detection = 10`.

1. Loading packages prints messages that are not needed in the report. Add
the chunk option `#| message: false` to the chunks that load packages, and
render the document. Are the messages gone?

2. Readers of the report may not want to see all the code. Add the chunk
options `#| code-fold: true` and `#| code-summary: "Show the code"` to the
chunk that calculates the alpha diversity. Render the document. How is the
code shown now?

3. Make the figure wider by adding `#| fig-width: 10` to the figure chunk.
Render the document.

**Useful resources:** [@sec-reproducible-reporting],
[Code cell options](https://quarto.org/docs/reference/cells/cells-knitr.html)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

The chunk options are added to the beginning of the chunks:

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| label: load-data
#| message: false
library(mia)
...
```

```{{r}}
#| message: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
# First, let's load some example data.
library(mia)
...
```

```{{r}}
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
library(miaViz)
plotBoxplot(
    tse,
    col.var = "observed_richness",
    x = "SampleType",
    colour.by = "Final_Barcode"
) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
    labs(x = "Sample types", y = expression(Richness[observed_richness]))
```
````

1. Yes. With `message: false`, the messages are not shown in the rendered
document, but the code is still run.

2. The code is hidden behind a clickable "Show the code" button, and the
reader can open it when needed. The output of the chunk is still shown.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Exercise 6: Tables and cross-references

**Goal:** Learn to add captions to figures and tables and to refer to them in
the text.

Continue with the document from Exercise 5.

1. Give the figure chunk the label `fig-richness` with `#| label:`, and add a
caption with `#| fig-cap:`.

2. Add a new code chunk that shows the sample type and the alpha diversity of
the first five samples as a table:

    ```r
    knitr::kable(
        as.data.frame(
            colData(tse)[1:5, c("SampleType", "observed_richness",
                "shannon_diversity")]
        )
    )
    ```

    Give the chunk the label `tbl-alpha`, add a caption with `#| tbl-cap:`, and
    hide its code with `#| echo: false`.

3. Under the figure and the table, write a sentence that refers to them with
`@fig-richness` and `@tbl-alpha`. Render the document.

4. Why must the labels of the figure and table chunks start with `fig-` and
`tbl-`?

**Useful resources:** [@sec-reproducible-reporting],
[Cross-references](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

The figure chunk and the new part of the document should look similar to the
following:

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| label: fig-richness
#| fig-cap: "Observed richness by sample type."
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
library(miaViz)
plotBoxplot(
    tse,
    col.var = "observed_richness",
    x = "SampleType",
    colour.by = "Final_Barcode"
) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
    labs(x = "Sample types", y = expression(Richness[observed_richness]))
```

```{{r}}
#| label: tbl-alpha
#| tbl-cap: "Sample type and alpha diversity of the first five samples."
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(
    as.data.frame(
        colData(tse)[1:5, c("SampleType", "observed_richness",
            "shannon_diversity")]
    )
)
```

@fig-richness shows the observed richness by sample type, and @tbl-alpha
lists the values of the first five samples.
````

3. In the rendered document, `@fig-richness` and `@tbl-alpha` are replaced by
clickable references, such as "Figure 1" and "Table 1".

4. Quarto uses the prefix of the label to recognize what the chunk produces.
Only chunks whose label starts with `fig-` or `tbl-` are numbered as figures
or tables, and only they can be cross-referenced. The caption is needed as
well for the cross-reference to work.
:::
::::
